findings.description: The parser uses inflateRawSync (synchronous decompression) inside an async method. A 50MB compressed XLSX can block the event loop for seconds. Should use async zlib.inflateRaw or offload to a worker thread.
Extracted text from <t> and <v> elements is not XML-unescaped. Entities like <, >, &, ", ' and numeric character references are passed through verbatim, corrupting cell values.
The r attribute (e.g. r="C1") is never parsed. Empty or missing cells cause column shifting — cells are packed contiguously instead of being placed at their correct column index.
Cells with t="inlineStr" contain <is><t>...</t></is> instead of <v>. The cell regex only captures <v> content, so inline string cells produce empty values.

When general purpose flag bit 3 is set, the parser scans byte-by-byte for the next signature (0x04034b50 or 0x02014b50). Compressed data can legitimately contain these byte sequences, causing premature truncation of entry data and corrupted output.

The parser only reads local file headers and never validates against the central directory (End of Central Directory record). A malicious file can craft local headers that differ from the central directory, causing the parser to read unintended data. Standard ZIP readers use the central directory as authoritative.
The cell regex <c\s+([^>]*)>(?:<v>...)?</c> requires a closing </c> tag. Self-closing empty cells like <c r="A1" s="0"/> are not matched and silently skipped.

Entries are stored in a Map keyed by name with last-wins semantics. A malicious XLSX could include a duplicate xl/sharedStrings.xml after the legitimate one, causing the parser to use attacker-controlled shared strings.
Regexes for <si>, <t>, <row>, <c>, <v> do not account for XML namespace prefixes (e.g., <x:si>). While most XLSX files omit prefixes in the body, namespace-qualified files would fail to parse.

IPv6 unspecified address '::' (equivalent to 0.0.0.0) is not covered by PRIVATE_IP_PATTERNS. On some OS configurations, connecting to '::' may reach localhost or local services, bypassing SSRF protection. The pattern /^0\./ catches 0.0.0.0 but there is no equivalent for '::'.

On 3xx redirect responses, the response stream is never consumed or destroyed before recursing. This leaves the underlying socket unconsumed, potentially causing socket pool exhaustion under repeated redirects with bodies. The response object should be destroyed (response.destroy() or response.resume()) before following the redirect.

HTTPS requests use hostname: pinnedIp without setting the 'servername' TLS option. This causes TLS SNI and certificate validation to be performed against the IP address rather than the original hostname. Most HTTPS servers will reject the connection or fail certificate validation, effectively breaking HTTPS. This functional deficiency may pressure developers to disable certificate validation (rejectUnauthorized: false) as a workaround, which would eliminate MITM protection. Fix by adding servername: url.hostname to the request options.

extractIPv4FromMapped only handles dotted-decimal IPv4-mapped IPv6 format (::ffff:a.b.c.d). If dns.lookup returns mapped addresses in hex format (e.g., ::ffff:7f00:1 for 127.0.0.1), the extraction fails and isPrivateIp returns false, potentially allowing connections to private IPs. Consider also parsing hex-form mapped addresses or normalizing all IPs before checking.

max_bytes and timeout_ms are not validated. A negative max_bytes would cause chunk slicing with negative length (producing empty buffer), and a zero or negative timeout_ms would immediately abort the request. Extremely large max_bytes values could cause excessive memory consumption. These should be clamped to reasonable bounds.

When multiple IPs are resolved, only resolvedIps[0] is used for the connection. If that IP is unreachable, the request fails without trying other resolved IPs. While not a security issue, it affects reliability. Additionally, IPv6 pinned IPs are passed directly as hostname without bracketing, which may cause connection failures for IPv6 targets.
